points.en: Prose method: learning through logical, sequential, outlined summaries, the method most used in preaching.
Visual method: learning through what the eye sees, such as drama, pictures and movement.
Story method: learning through symbols, using image and narrative as the vehicle that carries truth into the soul.
Danger of prose alone: information may be conveyed without being received, since people are not computers and the truth never lodges in the heart.
Left brain is the logical, analytical side (outline, argument); right brain is the creative side (image, metaphor, music, art).
Most preaching leans left, but hearers have both capacities and the gospel addresses the whole person, so the preacher must engage both.
Treats the model as a useful picture rather than strict science, and credits Andi Cook.
The left-brain outline simply organizes the information of the passage, such as what Jesus, the disciples and Peter did, or a keyword outline of application points.
The right-brain outline is built on a controlling metaphor drawn from the passage, such as the storms of life or taking your eyes off Jesus, which governs the whole sermon.
The difference in aim: the left-brain outline informs or instructs, while the right-brain picture lets the hearer feel and see the truth.
A controlling metaphor is the one overriding image or symbol, chosen first, that governs the development of the whole message.
It shapes the sermon by governing the introduction, movement, illustrations and conclusion, so the sermon is one image rather than a list of points.
Gives a worked example of a metaphor tied to a text and shows it making the truth visible.
Affirms that logic, doctrine and outline are God's gift and are not to be abandoned.
The imaginative approach does not replace truth but carries it to the heart; the danger is stopping at the analytical, so the choice between substance and imagination is false.
Notes that Jesus both reasoned and told stories.
People are not computers that download facts: information conveyed is not the same as information received, and truth must reach the heart, not only the ear.
Implication: prepare not only to be clear and correct but to be received, using image, story and the personal so the truth lodges.
Connects it to the idea that facts convince the mind but a story moves the heart.
Gives three metaphor examples from the unit, each stated as X is like Y with its text (for example temptation like fire, decision like a fence, discouragement like a steep mountain).
Explains for each how the picture opens its passage and makes the truth visible where bare statement could not.
The visual method opens a door to the heart that the ear cannot always open, as drama, pictures and acted parables show.
The visual must carry the truth and serve the text and message, never replace them or become spectacle for its own sake.
Most preaching leans left, toward defining, dividing and proving.
What is lost is the imaginative half of the hearer, where loves, fears and decisions live, so the truth may be correct yet unreceived.
Calls for engaging both hemispheres rather than abandoning the logical side.
Names a passage and one clear controlling metaphor, and states the truth it carries.
Shows how the introduction, movement and conclusion would all serve the one picture.
The metaphor rises out of the text and fits it honestly, rather than being imposed on it.
